description: ULAK is a two-member engineering team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We focus on radar, RF engineering, satellite remote sensing, signal processing, and software development. For the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge, we aim to develop an interactive application using NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite data to detect and visualize changes in Earth's surface, making complex scientific observations accessible and understandable.
summary:
ULAK — Beneath the Canopy is an open-source, interactive atlas that investigates seasonal radar changes in South Sudan’s cloud-covered Sudd wetlands using real NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band observations. Instead of assuming that every bright radar pixel means flooding, ULAK shows both the evidence and the uncertainty behind each interpretation.

We processed 10 NISAR acquisitions from 20 June to 18 October 2026; nine passed quality control. Users explore HH/HV time series, change, trend and persistence maps, compare dates, and open an Evidence Passport for each cell to inspect data provenance, quality checks, competing hypotheses and limitations.

In 155 cells consistently classified as inundated vegetation by the separate Sentinel-1-derived OPERA DSWx-S1 product, NISAR HH increased by 2.10 dB (95% CI 1.99–2.37), compared with 0.44 dB in 259 not-water cells. A strong eastern brightening zone was not similarly classified, revealing where radar interpretations diverge. These are associations, not confirmed flooding: vegetation and wet-canopy effects remain possible, and field validation is unavailable.

ULAK helps analysts, mappers and students identify changes worth investigating without confusing signals with certainty.
details:
Source code: https://github.com/h6q/ulak-sar-evidence-atlas

WHAT IT DOES

ULAK turns NISAR radar data into an evidence-first story for one of Africa's largest wetlands. In the web app a user can:

- play a quality-screened timeline of real NISAR HH and HV measurements of the central Sudd (stack 086_A_005, 20 June to 18 October 2026);

- switch between backscatter, first-to-last change, trend and strict-persistence layers;

- swipe between two dates and view change-hypothesis cells;

- click any 0.01-degree cell to see its measured time series and its Evidence Passport;

- export a study report and machine-readable JSON.

The Evidence Passport has eight parts: source, dates, measurement, observed change, quality checks, interpretation and uncertainty, independent context, and reasons the result might mislead. When the evidence does not decide between water and vegetation, the passport says "unresolved".

HOW IT WORKS

1. Catalog verification. Granule IDs, times, MD5 checksums and footprints of all 10 acquisitions are stored and re-checked against NASA's CMR catalog.

2. Real pixels, small download. Using the team's own Earthdata Login (entered at a hidden prompt, never stored), a Python pipeline range-reads only the study window (2224 x 2220 pixels at 20 m) of the HHHH and HVHV gamma0 layers from each NISAR GCOV HDF5 file instead of downloading 1.8 GB files. Each window is cached with a SHA-256 hash.

3. Compatibility and quality control. All dates share track, frame, mode, processing release (CRID P05023), map grid and units. A pattern-based rule (spatial correlation with the other dates) excludes one acquisition, 6 October, whose image is inconsistent with all others; the rule never looks at change magnitude. 24 September has HH only.

4. Analysis. 5 x 5 multilooking in linear power (100 m), then dB. Regions (permanent-wetland corridor, west margin, east margin) are fixed in advance from MODIS land cover, never from the radar change itself. Uncertainty uses spatial block bootstrap. Scene-wide (common-mode) change is always reported next to region-relative change.

5. Independent context. OPERA DSWx-S1 (Sentinel-1 C-band), OPERA DSWx-HLS (optical) and MODIS IGBP land cover were read as NASA GIBS renderings and decoded exactly from their published palettes. Eight NISAR dates have a DSWx-S1 date one day earlier.

6. Audit. Independent scripts recompute the headline numbers from the cached data (two-date audit 21/21 checks; time-series findings reproduced within 0.02 dB).

WHAT WE FOUND (9 quality-passed dates, 195,538 common 100 m cells, 1,955 km2)

- In the 155 analysis cells that DSWx-S1 classifies as inundated vegetation on all eight matched dates, NISAR HH rose by +2.10 dB between 20 June and 18 October (95% CI 1.99 to 2.37). In 259 cells classified not-water it rose +0.44 dB (0.38 to 0.50); in 48 open-water cells +0.65 dB (0.21 to 0.88).

- Among savanna cells, brightening peaks 10 to 14 km west (HH +2.77 dB) and 14 to 18 km east (+2.98 dB) of the wetland corridor centreline and is about zero at the centre.

- Relative to the scene-wide change, the corridor became darker (HH -0.91 dB, HV -1.10 dB) and the east margin brighter (HH +0.74 dB, HV +0.89 dB); confidence intervals exclude zero.

- Strict persistence (more than 3 dB in both raw and normalised series, on at least 75% of later dates including the last three) covers only 0.108% (HH) and 0.099% (HV) of the area: most large changes are episodic.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW

- DSWx-S1 is itself a radar-derived classification that also uses a land-cover map; it is not field truth. Agreement between two radar products is an association, not validated flooding.

- HV rose as well (+1.24 dB in the inundated-vegetation cells), so vegetation growth or rain-wet canopy cannot be separated from water. 125 of the 155 cells lie in one western belt, and the eastern peak is not mapped as inundated by DSWx-S1.

- First-to-last change in DSWx-S1 water fraction has near-zero spatial correlation with NISAR change (Spearman -0.003).

- The NISAR products are PROVISIONAL; the 20 June baseline has no matching DSWx-S1 date; no river-gauge or field data were available. We therefore make no flood-extent, flood-timing or accuracy claim.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Wetland and hydrology analysts can screen where L-band change deserves a gauge or field check.

- Humanitarian and conservation mappers can see which flood-like radar signals have independent support and which do not.

- Students and new NISAR users can learn to read HH/HV change on real data with laptop-scale downloads and open, tested code.

ULAK is a screening and learning tool, not an operational flood-warning system.

CREATIVITY AND WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Most change maps show a colour and leave the trust question to the viewer. ULAK attaches the evidence for and against each interpretation to every cell, keeps failed or missing inputs visible, and reports results that weaken its own story. We considered calibration drift, speckle, rain before each pass, wind on open water, cherry-picking of regions and thresholds, and the limits of optical data under vegetation.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, h5py, rasterio, pyproj, fsspec, aiohttp, Matplotlib, Pillow, pytest); JavaScript with Leaflet 1.9.4, HTML and CSS; PowerShell; Playwright for browser checks; PptxGenJS for the slides.

NEXT STEPS

Validate against river gauges, field observations and the original OPERA GeoTIFFs; investigate the 6 October acquisition at granule level; re-run with VALIDATED NISAR products; test incidence-angle and wind sensitivity.
